lessons.title: My new flat
lessons.description: Lucy writes about her small flat in the city centre.

material.body:
My name is Lucy and I am 24. I live in a small flat in the city centre. My flat has one bedroom, a kitchen and a bathroom. It is on the third floor, and there is no lift, so I walk up the stairs every day!

I love my flat because it is near my work. I walk to the office in ten minutes. There is a big park next to my building. On Sundays, I go running there with my friend Anna.

The flat is small, but it has a big window. From the window, I can see the river.

lessons.title: Saturday at the market
lessons.description: Tom goes to the market with his grandfather every week, but last Saturday was different.

material.body:
Every Saturday morning, Tom goes to the market with his grandfather. They leave home at eight o'clock and take the number 12 bus into town.

First, they buy fruit and vegetables. Tom's grandfather always talks to the man at the fruit stall — they have been friends for thirty years. Then they buy fresh bread from a small bakery near the church.

Last Saturday was different. It was raining, so there were not many people at the market. The fruit stall was closed because the owner was ill. Tom and his grandfather bought apples from a different stall, but his grandfather said they weren't as good.

Before going home, they always have hot chocolate at a café. Last Saturday, Tom paid for the drinks with his own money for the first time. His grandfather was very happy.

lessons.title: A weekend in Edinburgh
lessons.description: Jess writes an email to her friend about a weekend trip with her sister.

material.body:
Hi Maria,

Thanks for your email! I'm writing from Edinburgh — I'm here for the weekend with my sister Kate.

We arrived on Friday evening by train. The journey from London took four and a half hours, but it went quickly because we played cards all the way.

Yesterday we visited the castle. It's on a hill in the middle of the city, so the views are amazing. It was very windy, and Kate lost her hat! In the afternoon, we went to a museum because it started to rain.

Today the weather is better. We're going to walk up Arthur's Seat — it's an old volcano near the city. Then we're having dinner at a Scottish restaurant. I want to try haggis, but Kate says she'll just have fish!

We're going back to London tomorrow morning. Let's meet next week and I'll show you my photos.

Love,
Jess

lessons.title: My new hobby
lessons.description: A man who was bored in the evenings writes about learning pottery.

material.body:
Last year I decided to learn something new. I was 40, I worked in an office, and I was bored in the evenings. My wife suggested pottery — making bowls and cups from clay.

My first class was a disaster. My bowl fell off the wheel twice, and I had clay in my hair! But the teacher, Rosa, was very patient. She told me that everybody finds it difficult at the beginning.

Now I go to class every Wednesday evening. The class has eight students, and we are all different ages — the youngest is 19 and the oldest is 72. We often go for a pizza together after class.

Last month I made a set of six cups. They aren't perfect, but we use them every day at home. My next project is a big plate for my mother's birthday.

lessons.title: Why a short nap is good for you
lessons.description: An article about afternoon naps: how long to sleep and when.

material.body:
In many countries, an afternoon nap is a normal part of the day. But in places like the UK and the USA, sleeping during the day is often seen as lazy. Scientists now say that this attitude may be wrong.

Research shows that a short nap of 10 to 20 minutes can improve concentration and memory. After a nap, people make fewer mistakes and react more quickly. Some companies, including Google, have even created special rooms where employees can rest during their lunch break.

However, the length of the nap is important. If you sleep for more than 30 minutes, your body goes into deep sleep. When you wake up, you may feel tired and confused for up to an hour — scientists call this “sleep inertia”. Long naps late in the afternoon can also make it harder to fall asleep at night.

So what is the best way to nap? Experts suggest napping in the early afternoon, between 1 pm and 3 pm, when most people naturally feel sleepy. Find a quiet, dark place, set an alarm, and don't worry if you don't actually fall asleep — even resting with your eyes closed can help.

lessons.title: Review: The Blue Door café
lessons.description: A restaurant review: good food, fair prices — and one problem.

material.body:
I've walked past The Blue Door on Mill Street hundreds of times, but last Friday I finally went in — and I'm glad I did.

The café is tiny, with only six tables, so it's a good idea to book, especially at weekends. The decoration is simple: white walls, wooden furniture and, of course, a bright blue door. The owner, a former teacher called Dev, greeted us as if we were old friends.

The menu is short but interesting. I had the lentil soup, which was thick and full of flavour, and my partner chose the vegetable curry. Both came with warm homemade bread. For dessert, we shared a slice of chocolate cake. It was delicious, although a little too sweet for me.

My only complaint is the service, which was rather slow. We waited almost 40 minutes for our main courses, and there was only one waiter for the whole café. On the other hand, the prices are very reasonable: our meal for two cost £32, including drinks.

Overall, The Blue Door is a lovely place for a relaxed lunch — just don't go if you're in a hurry.

lessons.title: The dog at the supermarket
lessons.description: A short story: Mia finds a lost dog and tries to find its owner.

material.body:
When Mia found the dog, it was sitting outside the supermarket in the rain, shaking. It had a red collar but no name tag. Mia waited for twenty minutes, hoping that the owner would come back, but nobody did.

She took the dog home, dried it with an old towel and gave it some chicken. Her mother wasn't very pleased. “We can't keep it,” she said. “Someone must be looking for it.”

The next morning, Mia made posters with a photo of the dog and her phone number. She put them up at the supermarket, the bus stop and the vet's. She also posted the photo on a local website. For two days, nothing happened, and Mia secretly started to hope that she could keep the dog.

Then, on the third evening, her phone rang. It was an elderly man called Mr Hughes. He explained that his dog, Biscuit, had run away when a car alarm frightened her. He had been in hospital for a short operation, and his neighbour had been looking after Biscuit.

When Mr Hughes arrived, Biscuit ran straight to him. Mia felt sad, but also proud. A week later, a card arrived. Inside was a photo of Biscuit and a note: “Please come and visit us whenever you like.”

lessons.title: Podcast: life without a car
lessons.description: Sara sold her car two years ago. How does she get around now?

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Welcome back to City Life. My guest today is Sara, who sold her car two years ago. Sara, why did you decide to do that?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: Honestly, it started with money. I worked out that my car was costing me about three hundred pounds a month — insurance, fuel, parking, repairs. And I was only using it at weekends.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: So how do you get around now?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: Mostly by bike. My office is five kilometres away, so it takes me about twenty minutes. When it rains heavily, I take the tram.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Isn't it difficult with shopping?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: At first, yes. Now I do a big online order once a week and it's delivered. For small things, I just use my bike.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: What about longer trips?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: For holidays, I go by train, or I rent a car for a few days. It's much cheaper than owning one.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Is there anything you miss?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: Sometimes, yes. Visiting my parents is harder — they live in a village with only two buses a day. But overall, I feel healthier and I've saved a lot of money.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Definitely the weather. We work outside all year, even in the snow. And the job is very physical — carrying food, cleaning the areas.

segments.text: And the best part?

segments.text: Talking to visitors, especially children. Many of them have never seen a giraffe before. When they see how tall they are, their faces are amazing.

exercises.explanation: “Definitely the weather.”

exercises.prompt: Tom enjoys seeing children's reactions to the giraffes.
exercises.explanation: “When they see how tall they are, their faces are amazing.”

exercises.prompt: Tom says that young people should study ___.
exercises.explanation: “Study biology, and try to get some experience.”

lessons.title: Present Simple: he, she, it
lessons.description: With he, she and it, the verb gets -s: she works, he goes, it closes.

exercises.prompt: Match: I … → he …
exercises.explanation: he / she / it: + s (works), + es after o, sh, ch, s, x (goes, watches), y → ies (studies); have → has.

exercises.prompt: She ___ (work) in a bank.
exercises.explanation: she + work → works

exercises.prompt: My brother ___ (play) football on Sundays.
exercises.explanation: vowel + y → just + s: plays

exercises.prompt: Tom ___ (watch) TV every evening.
exercises.explanation: -ch → + es: watches

exercises.prompt: The shop ___ (close) at six.
exercises.explanation: it (the shop) + close → closes

exercises.prompt: My mum ___ coffee every morning.
exercises.explanation: she (my mum) → drinks

exercises.prompt: He ___ to school by bus.
exercises.explanation: go → goes (+ es after o)

exercises.prompt: My parents ___ in a small village.
exercises.explanation: they (my parents) → live, without -s
Subject + verb + object: My sister likes chocolate.
Emma plays the guitar.

lessons.title: At the restaurant
lessons.description: Words and phrases for ordering a meal and paying.

exercises.prompt: Match the words with their meanings.

pairs.menu: a list of the food in a restaurant
pairs.bill: the paper that shows how much you must pay
pairs.waiter: a person who brings food to your table
pairs.starter: a small dish before the main course
pairs.dessert: sweet food at the end of a meal

exercises.prompt: Can I see the ___, please? I want to choose my food.
exercises.explanation: You choose food from the menu.

exercises.prompt: We've finished our meal. Can we have the ___, please?
exercises.explanation: At the end, you ask for the bill and pay.

exercises.prompt: For ___, I'd like chocolate ice cream.
exercises.explanation: Ice cream at the end of a meal is dessert.

exercises.prompt: Waiter: Are you ready to ___? — Yes, I'd like the fish, please.
exercises.explanation: “Are you ready to order?” = do you know what you want to eat?

exercises.prompt: I'd like a ___ of water, please.
exercises.explanation: a glass / a bottle / a jug of water

exercises.prompt: Put the dialogue in order.
order: Good evening. A table for two?
Yes, please. By the window, if possible.
Of course. Here are your menus.

exercises.explanation: Could I have the bill? — a polite request.
